title: Fort Morgan Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Fort Morgan wells have a 99-foot median depth, with finished well costs modeled at $9,500-$17,400.
h1: Fort Morgan, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Fort Morgan means looking closely at the well permit, not just the listing description. Within 5 miles of Fort Morgan, Colorado DWR records include 2,125 permitted wells, with 1,558 recorded as constructed. The local records point to relatively shallow wells and generally strong reported yields, but the data is uneven: only 312 wells report a pump yield and 80 report a static water level.

This page covers well depth, production, water levels, permit history, estimated drilling cost, and the site checks that matter around Fort Morgan, Log Lane Village, Trail Side, Morgan Heights, Blue Sky, Saddle Ridge, and Brush.

sections.heading: Fort Morgan wells are usually shallow
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Fort Morgan is 99 feet. The middle half runs from 65 to 120 feet, so a driller bidding a typical site will usually be working in that range rather than planning for a very deep hole. Half of the recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 49% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Only 1% are between 300 and 600 feet, and none are recorded at 600 feet or deeper.

The deepest well in the records is 500 feet. Local permits most often name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 1,963 wells in that category. Alluvial and Quaternary Alluvium wells account for 70 and 48 records. The exact site still matters: plains sediment and fractured rock can change casing, grout, and drilling time from one lot to the next.

sections.heading: Reported well yields are strong, but verify the record
sections.html:
Among the 312 Fort Morgan-area wells that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is listed as 15.0 to 698.5 gallons per minute, and 94% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 1% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, 6% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 0% report under 1 gallon per minute.

That is encouraging for a buyer, but it does not guarantee the well on a particular parcel will perform the same way. Ask for the well construction report, pump test information, permitted use, and current equipment condition. A household-use exempt well is subject to Colorado rules, including the 35 gpm exempt-well pumping limit. Irrigation and other uses may require different water rights or approvals.

sections.heading: Water levels show no clear long-term drop
sections.html:
Only 80 wells in the local records report a static water level, so this part of the dataset is smaller than the depth and permit records. The median depth to water is 38 feet, with the middle half between 21 and 50 feet below the surface.

The decade comparison does not show a simple steadily dropping water table. The median was 30 feet below surface in the 1950s, 24 feet in the 2010s, and 32 feet in the 2020s. These measurements come from different wells and locations, so they are not a continuous reading from one monitoring point. For a purchase, have the existing well checked while it is under normal household demand and compare the measured water level with the construction report.

sections.heading: Permit history runs from early records to 2025
sections.html:
Fort Morgan has a long well-permit history. The records show 302 permits issued in the 1950s, 126 in the 1960s, 271 in the 1970s, 115 in the 1980s, 185 in the 1990s, 229 in the 2000s, 146 in the 2010s, and 68 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

Most permitted uses are domestic or household at 50%, followed by irrigation at 18%, stock at 15%, and monitoring at 12%. The most active names in the records are Canfield Drilling Company, also listed as Canfield, Harold E, with 389 records; Canfield, Leslie George, with 204; and Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 161. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation or proof of current availability.

sections.heading: A typical Fort Morgan well costs more than the hole
sections.html:
For the alluvium and plains sedimentary rock described in the local cost model, drilling is estimated at $35 to $55 per foot. At the 99-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone models to about $3,500 to $5,400.

A usable water system includes more than drilling. The local model puts a finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical at about $9,500 to $17,400. Treat that as a planning range, not a fixed bid. Access, casing and grout requirements, difficult ground, water testing, pump size, electrical distance, and the final well depth can move the price. Get a written proposal that separates drilling from completion and identifies what happens if the hole does not produce enough water.

sections.heading: Check contamination, septic layout, and dry-hole risk
sections.html:
Environmental review deserves attention around Fort Morgan. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 24 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. No historic mine features are mapped in that area. These records do not prove a private well is contaminated, but they are a reason to test existing water and review nearby land uses before closing.

Low yield is not prominent in the reported records, yet a dry hole or poor-producing interval remains a site-specific risk, especially where fractured rock is involved. Confirm the well location, casing and grout details, septic system, replacement area, and proposed building footprint. Keep the well and septic layout compliant with applicable separation requirements, and check whether the permitted use supports the house, livestock, irrigation, or future plans.

sections.heading: Use nearby wells to price and investigate the lot
sections.html:
Before buying near Fort Morgan, pull the DWR permit and construction records for the parcel and compare them with nearby wells in Log Lane Village, Trail Side, Morgan Heights, Blue Sky, Saddle Ridge, and Brush. Neighboring records can help establish a realistic depth and yield range, but they are not a guarantee for your lot.

For an existing home, ask for a flow test, pressure-tank inspection, pump information, water-quality testing, and evidence that the use matches the permit. For vacant land, get a driller's site review before relying on a cost allowance. If the intended use is more than ordinary household service, check water-rights requirements early. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be needed for some uses.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Fort Morgan?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth within 5 miles of Fort Morgan is 99 feet. The middle half runs from 65 to 120 feet. Half of the recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 49% are between 100 and 300 feet. The deepest record is 500 feet, so a specific parcel still needs its own permit and site review.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Fort Morgan?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 99-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $3,500 to $5,400. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $9,500 to $17,400. Access, ground conditions, final depth, and equipment can change the written bid.

faq.q: How much water do Fort Morgan wells produce?
faq.a: Of the 312 local wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The records show 94% above 15 gallons per minute, 6% between 5 and 15, 1% between 1 and 5, and 0% under 1. Reported yields are useful screening information, not a guarantee for an untested well.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Fort Morgan?
faq.a: Safety depends on the individual well and its surroundings. Within about 10 miles, records show 24 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not establish contamination in a private well. Test existing water, review nearby land uses, and inspect the well, casing, grout, and septic layout before purchase.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Fort Morgan?
faq.a: The available measurements do not show a simple steady decline. Median depth to water was 30 feet in the 1950s, 24 feet in the 2010s, and 32 feet in the 2020s. Only 80 wells report static water levels, and the measurements come from different locations. Treat the series as local context, not a continuous monitoring record.
